question:
Patient note:
A 63-year-old man with a twenty-year history of alcohol use averaging a pint of spirits daily until he entered a rehabilitation program nine months ago came to the university liver clinic at 10 a.m. for an unscheduled visit because over the past three weeks his partner observed that he had begun misplacing car keys, dozing off after breakfast, and taking noticeably longer to calculate tips at their café, though he still recognized acquaintances and navigated public transport without assistance; he had also complained that by late evening his waistband felt a bit snugger than in the morning and that rolling from his back to either side produced a faint sloshing sensation deep within his abdomen, yet he denied frank abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, gastrointestinal bleeding, lower-extremity swelling, fevers, chills, chest discomfort, dyspnea, syncope, or weight change. His cirrhosis had been diagnosed four years earlier when screening imaging for elevated γ-glutamyl transferase revealed a nodular contour and splenomegaly; he had undergone two uncomplicated sessions of endoscopic variceal band ligation at that time but had never required therapeutic paracentesis, non-selective β-blockers, ammonia-lowering agents, or vitamin K injections. Additional medical history included well-controlled primary hypertension treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily, mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease from a 25-pack-year cigarette habit ceased six years ago, and degenerative lumbar disc disease managed with physical therapy; surgical history was limited to an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy twelve years prior. He denied illicit drug use, had no known drug allergies, and his current medication list consisted of amlodipine, a chewable multivitamin, and over-the-counter famotidine 20 mg as needed for heartburn; he took no anticoagulants, diuretics, herbal supplements, or psychoactive agents. He lived with his partner, walked a dog for thirty minutes each morning, and adhered to a low-salt diet recommended by the clinic dietitian. Family history was notable for a father who died of esophageal carcinoma at 70 years and a mother with type 2 diabetes; no relatives had liver disease. On presentation—before venipuncture, intravenous access, imaging, or administration of any medication—vital signs read temperature 36.9 °C, blood pressure 124/68 mm Hg, heart rate 82 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97 % breathing ambient air. The patient sat upright, greeted staff appropriately, and was oriented to person, place, and approximate date but needed ten seconds to recall the name of the clinic physician; he recited the months of the year in reverse order with two pauses and produced slightly tremulous handwriting on the intake form. Cranial nerves II–XII were intact, motor strength was 5/5 throughout, sensation was normal, reflexes were symmetric, and when asked to extend his arms and cock his wrists a subtle flapping motion appeared after fifteen seconds. Sclerae displayed a light golden hue, there were half a dozen spider telangiectasias across the anterior chest, and breath carried a faint sweet odor. Jugular venous pulsation measured 7 cm H₂O at 30°, carotid pulses were brisk, the cardiac exam revealed a regular rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and lung fields were clear to auscultation. The abdominal wall had a gentle outward curve yet the umbilicus remained slightly indented; percussion produced tympany over the epigastrium that transitioned to a slender rim of dullness in the dependent right flank, which shifted when he rolled to the opposite side, and with an assistant’s hand along the midline a soft impulse was transmitted across the abdominal wall. The liver edge felt firm and finely nodular 1 cm below the costal margin on deep inspiration, the spleen tip was not palpable, bowel sounds were normoactive, and there was no rebound or guarding. Lower extremities showed no pitting edema, cyanosis, or clubbing. Capillary glucose measured 106 mg/dL. Point-of-care ultrasonography performed immediately—still prior to phlebotomy or any therapeutic intervention—demonstrated a shrunken heterogeneous liver with capsular irregularity, hepatopetal portal flow of 17 cm/s without thrombus, a spleen measuring 15 cm in craniocaudal length, and a barely perceptible anechoic stripe of free fluid less than 2 cm deep tracking along the right paracolic gutter; kidneys were of normal size with preserved corticomedullary differentiation, and no biliary dilation or focal masses were seen. A portable upright chest radiograph obtained moments later displayed clear lung fields and elevated hemidiaphragms but no pleural effusion, while a 12-lead electrocardiogram recorded normal sinus rhythm at 80 beats/min with a QTc of 418 ms. Peripheral venous blood drawn seconds later—documented before any vitamin K, albumin infusion, diuretic, laxative, antimicrobial, or sedative—revealed: total bilirubin 2.15 mg/dL, serum albumin 3.13 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 42 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 68 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 152 U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 210 U/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 15 mg/dL, creatinine 0.94 mg/dL (estimated GFR 84 mL/min/1.73 m²), hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, white blood cell count 5.6 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 118 × 10⁹/L, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 1.62. Urinalysis demonstrated moderate bilirubin, trace urobilinogen, no protein, and no evidence of infection. Serum ammonia, hepatitis serologies to exclude coincident viral infection, and α-fetoprotein were sent and were pending at the time this note was completed. Up to this point the patient had received no pharmacologic or procedural therapy, so all findings above represent his untreated physiologic state at the moment of presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Child-Pugh Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Child-Pugh score assigns 1–3 points to each of five findings. Use the untreated admission findings:
- Total bilirubin: 2.15 mg/dL is in the 2–3 mg/dL range → 2 points.
- Albumin: 3.13 g/dL is in the 2.8–3.5 g/dL range → 2 points.
- INR: 1.62 is below 1.7 → 1 point.
- Ascites: shifting dullness and a thin stripe of free fluid on ultrasound indicate mild ascites → 2 points.
- Encephalopathy: slowed calculations, daytime drowsiness and subtle asterixis with preserved orientation fit grade I–II → 2 points.
Total: 2 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 9 (Child-Pugh class B).
Final answer: 9
